items.prompt: What does the standard deviation describe?

items.prompt: Two dice are rolled. Which total has the most ways to occur?
items.explanation: Seven has 6 of 36 combinations; 2 and 12 have one each.

items.prompt: A sum of many small independent parts tends to look like what?
items.explanation: This is the Central Limit Theorem.

items.prompt: Part A has mean 3 and part B has mean 5, independent. The sum has mean...

items.prompt: Independent parts have variances 2 and 3. The sum has variance...

items.prompt: Why are totals in the middle more common for two dice?

items.prompt: Is the shape of one die roll a bell?

items.prompt: Six independent delays are added. Total mean is...
items.explanation: Means add for sums.

items.prompt: Which name matches 'sums of independent parts tend toward a bell'?
items.explanation: That is what the theorem states.

items.prompt: Expected count 50 and observed 64, with sd 6.12. About how many sds out?
items.explanation: 14 divided by 6.12.

items.prompt: A z-score of 1 is usually...
items.explanation: About one sd out is routine.

items.prompt: Which z-score is the most suspicious?
items.explanation: Larger distance from the mean is rarer.

items.prompt: An alert fires at a threshold just above the mean. What happens?
choices: It only fires on real faults
items.explanation: Close-to-mean thresholds are crossed all the time by chance.

items.prompt: Failures come in bursts. Are the trials independent?
items.explanation: Bursts mean one failure raises the chance of others.

items.prompt: A result is 2.3 sds out once. The sensible verdict is...

items.prompt: Z-score is computed as...
items.explanation: Gap divided by typical wobble.

items.prompt: Which makes an alert threshold more meaningful?
choices: Placing it far into the tail
items.explanation: Far thresholds are rarely crossed by luck.

items.prompt: A latency is continuous uniform from 2 ms to 10 ms. What is the chance it falls between 4 ms and 6 ms?
choices: 25%, since the slice is 2 ms of an 8 ms range
20%, since the slice is 2 ms of a 10 ms range
50%, since 4 to 6 sits in the centre of the range
33%, since three equal slices cover the range
items.explanation: The range is 10 − 2 = 8 and the slice is 2 long, so 2/8 = 25%.
items.reference:
Uniform: equal pieces get equal chance
🎲 discrete: N listed outcomes, each 1/N (die face = 1/6)
📏 continuous: interval length / total length
🎯 one exact decimal value: probability 0
Why: uniform means no outcome or equal-sized slice is favoured, so counting size is all you need.
items.learnMore:
Uniform distributions

Discrete uniform: probability is one over the number of outcomes. Continuous uniform on [a, b]: probability of an interval is its length divided by b minus a.

Common mistake

Thinking a uniform process gives perfectly even counts. Equal chances do not mean equal results in a small sample.
items.reflection: Think of a lottery, a shuffled playlist or a random seating chart. What would it mean for it to be uniform, and how even would you expect a short run of it to look?

items.explanation: With infinitely many possible values no single one gets a positive share, so intervals carry the probability.

items.prompt: 600 fair die rolls: mean sixes 100, sd about 9.13. A count of 118 is about how many sds out?
items.reference:
Binomial: counting yeses in n trials
📍 mean = n × p
↔️ standard deviation = √(n × p × (1 − p))
📐 z = (observed − mean) / standard deviation
🎲 60 rolls, p = 1/6: mean 10, sd about 2.89
Why: the standard deviation sets what a normal gap looks like, so a z-score turns a raw gap into a comparable number.
items.learnMore:
Binomial mean and spread

With n independent trials of equal chance p, the count of successes averages n times p and wanders by about the square root of n p (1 - p). Both assumptions, same p and independence, matter.

Common mistake

Judging a gap by its raw size. A gap of 5 is large for a standard deviation of 2.9 and small for one of 10.
items.reflection: Think of something you count over a fixed number of tries, such as free throws made or emails answered quickly. What is the mean, and how much wobble would you call normal before suspecting something changed?

items.prompt: Four independent parts each have variance 4 (sd 2). What is the sd of the total?
items.explanation: Variances add to 16, whose square root is 4.
items.reference:
Sums of independent parts
➕ means add
➕ variances add (not standard deviations)
🔔 the total bunches in the middle
🎲 two dice: 1 way to make 2, 6 ways to make 7
Why: middle totals can be reached by more combinations than extreme ones, and independent parts partly cancel.
items.learnMore:
Central Limit Theorem

A sum of many independent, small random parts tends toward a bell curve whatever the shape of each part. For the total, add the means and add the variances.

Common mistake

Adding standard deviations. Four independent parts each with standard deviation 2 give a total of 4, not 8.
items.reflection: Think of a trip or a project built from several independent stages. Which stages could you add up by mean and variance, and which are tangled together enough that the rule would not hold?

items.prompt: Server 3 got 64 of 200 at p = 1/4 (z 2.29, about 1.5% chance). Why is it more likely that SOME server looks this odd?
choices: Any of 4 servers could have been picked
The other servers always read lower than it
The variance changes once you look at data
Chance is paid back over a long enough time
items.explanation: Four candidate servers each had a chance to look odd, up to about 4 × 1.5%.
items.reference:
Reading a gap with z-scores
⚖️ 64 of 200 at p = 1/4: z about 2.29
🔔 500 requests, p = 0.02: threshold 20 is z about 3.19 (0.31%)
🔗 correlated failures break the independent-trial math
🔍 picking the target after the data inflates surprise
Why: decide what is suspicious by how many standard deviations out, using assumptions that actually hold.
items.learnMore:
Thresholds and verdicts

A z-score under about 2 is ordinary wobble, 2 to 3 is worth watching, and well beyond 3 suggests the process itself changed. Thresholds belong in the tail; they depend on independence.

Common mistake

Calling a result impossible because it is odd. A z-score of 2.3 happens by chance regularly across many checks.
items.reflection: Think of an alarm you have learned to ignore, such as a phone alert, a car warning or a dashboard flag. Was its threshold too close to normal wobble, and what would a better threshold look like?

Dividing by the variance instead of its square root, or forgetting the (1 - p) factor.
items.reflection: Think of a count you track in daily life, such as steps, sales or late buses. How would you decide a bad week was bad luck rather than a real change?
